area: Area IX. Performance and Ground Reference Maneuvers
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the purpose and procedure of the steep spiral and its tie to emergency landings, demonstrate it from the right seat while explaining it (bank never past 60°, specified airspeed ±10 knots, rollout ±10°, finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL), and spot, explain and fix the errors your learners make.
why: The steep spiral teaches a pilot to lose a lot of altitude quickly while staying over one spot, the same skill that gets an engine-out airplane down over a good field to the key position [[24:212|AFH 10-3]] [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. It packs wind correction, airspeed control in a gliding turn and engine care into a few minutes of descent. As the instructor you fly it while talking, watch a learner fly it, and catch the drift or speed error before it becomes a dive near the ground.

warmup: Think first: your learner's steep spiral looks fine on the first lap. By the third lap the circle has slid downwind of the silo, the airspeed swings 15 knots between upwind and downwind, and the altimeter shows 1,700 feet AGL with half a turn to go. Which of those three problems would you fix first, what single cue would you give for each, and when should you have noticed them?

key_terms.def: A gliding turn at constant radius around a ground reference, flown for at least three 360° turns to lose altitude quickly over a selected spot, finishing no lower than 1,500 feet AGL [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].
Speed over the ground. It is lower than airspeed headed upwind and higher headed downwind [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].
A turn whose ground track stays a fixed distance from a point. In wind it needs a bank that changes with groundspeed [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].
The sideways movement of the airplane with the air mass; it is the same number of miles per hour whatever the airspeed [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
A turn with power off. It needs more back pressure than a straight glide or level turn and lighter rudder than powered flight [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].
The airspeed that gives the greatest forward distance for a given loss of altitude in still air, at the highest lift-to-drag ratio [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].
Periodically advancing the throttle for a few seconds during a long idle glide to avoid overcooling, plug fouling and carburetor ice [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
An anti-icing system that preheats the air before the carburetor. It lowers engine power, sometimes up to 15 percent [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
The point where a power-off approach to a field becomes a normal power-off approach; the downwind key is where the throttle is closed abeam the landing spot [[24:198|AFH 9-27]] [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].
A maneuver to descend as soon and as fast as possible without exceeding structural limits, usually in a 30 to 45° bank with drag devices as recommended [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].
A nose-low descending turn in which airspeed and G-load build quickly, often from a botched turn [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
An illusion in a long coordinated turn: the pilot senses wings level, sees the altitude drop, pulls back and tightens the spiral [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]] [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

chunks.title: Purpose, procedure and the CFI standard

body.p: The steep spiral is a way to get rid of a lot of altitude quickly while staying over one chosen spot, and it can be useful during an emergency landing. It is a gliding turn that holds a constant radius around a point on the ground, like turns around a point, except the airplane is descending fast. It takes at least three 360° turns and should start high enough to finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL [[24:212|AFH 10-3]].

The procedure in one breath: clear the airspace, close the throttle, apply carburetor heat if equipped, and slow to gliding speed. Then lower the nose and roll into the bank as the reference point is reached. Your distance from the point sets the radius, and the steepest bank must not pass 60°. Steepen on downwind headings and shallow on upwind headings, clear the engine now and then, and lead airspeed changes with pitch. After at least three turns, roll out toward a definite object or on a specific heading, into a wings-level glide with no change in airspeed, then recover to cruise [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

head: What the examiner sees
CFI ACS wording
rows: Clearing (S1)
Clear the area. (ACS AI.IX.B.S1)
Altitude plan (S2)
Select an altitude sufficient to continue through a series of at least three, 360° turns. (ACS AI.IX.B.S2)
The spiral (S3)
Establish and maintain a steep spiral, not to exceed 60° angle of bank, to maintain a constant radius about a suitable ground reference point. (ACS AI.IX.B.S3)
Wind correction (S4)
Apply wind-drift correction to track a constant radius circle around selected reference point with bank not to exceed 60° a steepest point in turn. (ACS AI.IX.B.S4)
Attention (S5)
Divide attention between airplane control, traffic avoidance and the ground track while maintaining coordinated flight. (ACS AI.IX.B.S5)
Tolerances (S6)
Maintain the specified airspeed, ±10 knots and roll out toward an object or specified heading, ±10°, and complete the maneuver no lower than 1,500 feet above ground level (AGL). (ACS AI.IX.B.S6)
Teaching (S7)
Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task. (ACS AI.IX.B.S7)

body.p: What is new for you: the skills line says the applicant 'demonstrates and simultaneously explains', and S7 asks you to analyze and correct errors, so expect the examiner to fly a flawed spiral as your learner. The flight numbers are not new. The commercial ACS uses the same wording for clearing, altitude, bank, wind correction, attention and the ±10 knot, ±10°, 1,500 feet AGL limits (ACS CA.V.B.S1 to S6), so your commercial learners fly to exactly the standard you demonstrate. The private ACS has no steep spiral Task.

callout.text: For an ASEL CFI test, the evaluator must select at least four Area IX Tasks, including Task A (Steep Turns) or Task B (Steep Spiral) (ACS Area IX note). Load factor, accelerated stalls and overbanking are taught in the Steep Turns lesson (AI.IX.A); this lesson only applies them to the spiral.

check.q: Which parts of the CFI steep spiral standard go beyond what your commercial learner is tested on?
check.a: Explaining while you demonstrate, and analyzing and correcting common errors (ACS AI.IX.B.S7). The flight tolerances match the commercial ACS (ACS CA.V.B.S1 to S6).

chunks.title: Why it exists: getting down over a field

body.p: Relationship to emergency landing procedures: after a power failure, a pilot may use any mix of normal gliding maneuvers, from wings level to spirals, to arrive at the normal key position at normal traffic pattern altitude over the chosen field. From the key point on, it is a normal power-off approach [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. The steep spiral is the practice version of the 'spiral down over the field' part.

bullets: High altitude has its own trap: with more fields to choose from, an inexperienced pilot may delay the decision, and with lots of altitude to use, errors in maneuvering and glide estimates creep in [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. Application: the spiral keeps the learner over one field instead of wandering.
A constant gliding speed matters because speed changes spoil any judgment of glide distance and landing spot [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

Rolling out on a heading perpendicular to the wind or directly into it, instead of toward an object, makes the exercise harder and is a particularly useful skill in an actual emergency [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
Noting the altitude lost on each revolution tells the pilot when to roll out so as not to be too high or too low for a safe approach [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
The base key position is not a fixed landmark; vary altitude and location in training so learners do not tie it to a particular tree or crossroad [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

head: Steep spiral
Emergency descent
rows: Goal
Lose altitude while staying over a selected spot [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]
Descend as soon and as rapidly as possible without exceeding structural limits [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Bank
Varies with wind; steepest not over 60° [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]
About 30 to 45° to keep positive load factors [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Power and speed
Idle, carburetor heat if equipped, gliding speed held constant [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]
Idle unless the manufacturer prohibits it; the maximum allowable airspeed for the procedure, never past VNE, VLE or VFE [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Configuration
The AFH spiral text does not say [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]
Gear and flaps as the manufacturer recommends, for maximum drag [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]
Engine
Clear it periodically to avoid overcooling, plug fouling and carburetor ice [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]
Avoid prolonged practice so the cylinders do not cool too much [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]

body.p: The AFH itself warns that the two maneuvers are similar but used for different reasons, usually at different airspeeds and configurations [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. Learners mix them up, so teach them on different days or contrast them on purpose.

callout.text: The AIH suggests prompting the learner, before a ground reference maneuver, to name collision hazards and a safe place for an emergency landing [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. For the spiral, make the field part of the setup: 'That field is our engine-out field. Tell me the wind and how you would end up on downwind key.'

check.q: Your learner asks why the examiner might ask for a rollout into the wind instead of toward a barn. What do you tell them?
check.a: It is the harder version, and the AFH calls it particularly useful in an actual emergency [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

chunks.title: Wind, groundspeed and the ground track

body.p: Effects of wind on ground track: the airplane moves with the air mass. At 90 knots in a 10-knot crosswind it drifts 10 nautical miles sideways every hour, and at 180 knots it still drifts 10 [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Headed upwind the groundspeed drops, headed downwind it rises, and the effect is largest when the wind is along the airplane's long axis [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

In wind, a fixed bank no longer draws a circle over the ground. As groundspeed rises the radius over the ground grows, and as it falls the radius shrinks, so a constant radius takes a changing bank [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

Show it before you teach the spiral. The AFH demonstration: pick a road or railroad parallel to the wind, fly into the wind over it, and make a 360° turn at a constant medium bank. You come back over the road, but downwind of where you started. Over a road with a crosswind, the same turn drifts away from it. Either way the path over the ground is not a circle, even though through the air it was a perfect one [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

bullets: Pilots do not calculate drift corrections for ground reference maneuvers; they watch the references and adjust to cancel the drift [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]. Teach eyes outside, not math in the air.
The wind can change during the descent; the AFH says to keep correcting for changes in wind direction and velocity throughout the spiral [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
Wind changes the glide over the ground too: a tailwind carries the airplane farther and a headwind shortens the glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]], which matters when the spiral ends at a field.
Find the wind before you start from windsocks, smoke, dust, fires, wind farms or patterns on water [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

callout.text: Risk of wind (application): a strong wind makes the bank needed headed downwind steeper. If the learner chooses a tight circle, the airplane can need more than the 60° the ACS allows (ACS AI.IX.B.S3, S4), and a learner chasing the circle may overbank. Size the circle for the wind before the roll-in.

check.q: On the first lap the circle stays put, but on the third lap, much lower, it starts sliding. The learner has not changed anything. What do you tell them?
check.a: The wind may be different at the lower altitude; the AFH says to keep correcting for changes in wind direction and velocity during the spiral [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

chunks.title: Holding a constant radius about the point

body.p: Maintaining a constant radius about a point: the radius is set by your distance from the point when you roll in, and it can only be held by correcting for drift, steepening the bank on downwind headings and shallowing it on upwind headings [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. It is the same rule as turns around a point: higher groundspeed, steeper bank; lower groundspeed, shallower bank [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

The AFH numbers make it concrete: 90 knots airspeed in a 10-knot wind, so 100 knots groundspeed downwind and 80 knots upwind. Downwind, a 45° bank gives a radius over the ground of about 890 feet. As the groundspeed drops, the bank must come down, to about 33° at the upwind point, to keep that same 890 feet [[24:150|AFH 7-4]]. At higher groundspeed there is less time to get around, so the steeper bank raises the rate of turn to make up for it [[24:150|AFH 7-4]]. The PHAK radius formula is radius = speed squared / (11.26 x tangent of bank) [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]; application: with groundspeed in it, it reproduces the AFH numbers.

bullets: Heading versus position: in the downwind half the heading leads toward the inside of the circle; in the upwind half it lags toward the outside [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].
Choose a prominent reference that is easy to see but small enough to be precise [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].
In a high-wing airplane the lowered wing can hide the point, especially in left turns flown from the left seat; change the altitude or the radius so the point stays in view [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].

Sizing the circle (application): the steepest bank comes on the downwind heading, and the ACS caps it at 60° at the steepest point (ACS AI.IX.B.S4), so choose a radius that needs less than that with room to spare.

callout.text: Fast over the ground, steep. Slow over the ground, shallow. Downwind half, nose in; upwind half, nose out.

check.q: In the AFH example, why does the bank come down from 45° to about 33° between the downwind and upwind points?
check.a: Groundspeed falls from 100 to about 80 knots (90 knots airspeed, 10-knot wind), and a constant radius over the ground needs less bank at lower groundspeed [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

chunks.title: Airspeed control and coordination in the gliding turn

body.p: Holding the specified airspeed is the skill learners find hardest. Airspeed tends to wander as the bank changes, so the pilot has to anticipate a pitch correction with every bank change [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Three things push the nose down and the speed up in a gliding turn: lift tilted by the bank, too much rudder because control pressures feel light, and the airplane's natural nose-down tendency with power off. So a gliding turn takes more back pressure than a straight glide or a level turn [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

Application: in the spiral the bank changes all the way around, so the pitch does too. Steepening toward downwind, raise the nose a little; shallowing toward upwind, relax it. If the learner only moves the ailerons, the speed rises downwind and decays upwind every lap.

bullets: Uncoordinated flight: rudder forces are lighter in a glide, and learners used to powered flight press too hard, causing slips and skids [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].
The airplane's built-in correction for P-factor and slipstream stays in a glide, so slight left rudder is likely needed to stay coordinated [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Sound is an airspeed cue: more noise means more speed. Teach the learner to cross-check sound, sight and control pressure [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Trim once the speed is stable to take out held pressures [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Coming out of a gliding turn, release the back pressure used in the turn, or the nose pitches up and speed drops [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

callout.text: A low gliding steep turn with rudder pushed into the bank while the pilot pulls to save altitude can quickly become an unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. The spiral at altitude is where you fix rudder habits before they meet the ground.

check.q: Your learner holds airspeed well on the upwind side but is 12 knots fast every time the airplane heads downwind. What is the cause and the coaching cue?
check.a: The bank steepens downwind and nothing was done with pitch; a gliding turn needs more back pressure as the bank increases, so lead each bank change with a pitch change [[24:213|AFH 10-4]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

chunks.title: Keeping the engine alive in a long idle descent

body.p: A long glide at idle can overcool the engine, foul the spark plugs or let carburetor ice form. To prevent it, advance the throttle now and then and hold it for a few seconds; a cylinder head temperature gauge, if installed, shows how the engine is cooling. When you advance the throttle, adjust the pitch to keep the airspeed constant, preferably while headed into the wind [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

bullets: If carburetor icing conditions are suspected and closed-throttle operation is planned, put the carburetor heat full on before closing the throttle and leave it on [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
Open the throttle smoothly for a few seconds now and then to keep the engine warm, or the carburetor heater may not make enough heat [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
Carburetor ice is particularly dangerous at reduced power in a descent and can build unnoticed until power is added [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

In simulated emergencies, keep the engine warm and cleared, and make sure either you or the learner clearly has the throttle; misunderstandings about it have caused many near accidents [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].
Clearing the engine is not stretching the glide: using the throttle to increase the glide instead of merely clearing the engine is a listed power-off approach error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

callout.text: Sample patter (application): 'Headed into the wind now. Throttle up for a few seconds, nose up a touch to hold our speed, and back to idle. Carb heat stays on.' Brief before the flight who touches the throttle.

check.q: Why does the learner have to change pitch when clearing the engine?
check.a: The power burst would change the airspeed; the AFH says to adjust the pitch to keep a constant airspeed when advancing the throttle [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

body.p: Airframe or airspeed limitations: the bank limit is 60° (ACS AI.IX.B.S3, S4). In a level turn, 60° already doubles the load factor, and stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]; the Steep Turns lesson has the details. The PHAK names the danger directly: stalling by accident when the load factor goes up, as in a steep turn or spiral [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]]. Before the flight, look up the POH stall speed at the steepest bank you expect, so you know your margin [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

Airspeed limits come from the airspeed indicator: the red line is VNE, beyond which structural damage could occur, and the yellow arc from VNO to VNE is for smooth air only, and then only with caution [[1:232|PHAK 9-2]]. A proper spiral stays at gliding speed, far below them. A botched one does not: a spiral dive is a nose-low descending turn in which airspeed and G-load build quickly, often from a botched turn [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. The AFH also lists high-speed steep spirals following botched steep level turns as a case of an unrecoverable sink rate [[24:103|AFH 4-17]].

bullets: A startled pilot who pulls back hard while rolling level can load the airframe enough to damage or break it [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

Push a little forward elevator to about +1 G before rolling level: it lowers the angle of attack and the G-load and prevents a rolling pullout, which exceeds the design limit more easily [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
The airplane may be at or past VNE, so raise the nose slowly and gently [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].
Listed recovery errors include not reducing power first, pulling out without rolling level, pulling and rolling at the same time, and not unloading before rolling level [[24:132|AFH 5-27]].

callout.text: With anyone other than a crewmember aboard, no pilot may make an intentional maneuver that exceeds 60° of bank or 30° nose-up or nose-down unless each occupant wears an approved parachute. This does not apply to flight tests for a certificate or rating, or to maneuvers required for a certificate or rating when given by a CFI or by an ATP instructing under 14 CFR 61.67 [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]]. A spiral flown to the standard never exceeds 60° of bank (ACS AI.IX.B.S3). Application: a gliding attitude is far from 30° nose-down, so a proper spiral stays inside the rule; one that steepens past 60° or becomes a nose-low dive does not, so a learner practicing with a passenger aboard must not let it.

check.q: Your learner's spiral has become a nose-low, steep-bank dive with the speed building. Why must a little forward elevator come before rolling level?
check.a: It unloads the wing to about +1 G, lowering angle of attack and G-load, and prevents a rolling pullout, which exceeds the design limit more easily [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

body.p: Build it from blocks. Performance maneuvers should wait until the pilot shows consistent competency in the fundamentals, begin with a detailed ground lesson, and use segmented building blocks with enough repetition [[24:210|AFH 10-1]]. The spiral is a gliding turn around a point [[24:212|AFH 10-3]], so the blocks are the normal glide, gliding turns and turns around a point. When a new skill relates to ones already learned, the AIH recommends the known-to-unknown strategy [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]: 'This is turns around a point, power off, three times, going down.'

On the ground, cover the objective and completion standard, the exact actions and the end result, and the safety procedures [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. For the spiral that means: the ACS numbers, the wind map (where the steepest and shallowest bank will be), the circle size, the airspeed, the engine-clearing plan and who has the throttle, the altitude plan, the rollout heading, and the spiral dive recovery if it goes wrong.

head: Point in the maneuver
Sample patter (application)
Basis
rows: Before entry
'Clear left, right, above and below, especially below. Carb heat on, throttle idle, holding altitude until we slow to our gliding speed.'
Roll-in at the point
'The point is off the wingtip; nose down to hold the speed, rolling in. This distance is our radius.'
Turning downwind
'Groundspeed is building, so the bank steepens, and I raise the nose a little to keep the speed.'
Turning upwind
'Slower over the ground, bank shallower, ease the back pressure. Into the wind: clear the engine.'
Each lap
'Lap one done: we lost about this much. Two more laps puts us here, above our floor.'
Rollout
'Lead the heading, wings level, release the back pressure, same speed. Now recover to cruise.'

bullets: Demonstrate it exactly the way you want it practiced, safety steps included, in the order you briefed it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].
When the learner talks you through a spiral while you fly, listen for whether they know where downwind is before they are busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Make the first spirals correct ones; what is learned first sticks [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Teach on the ground, coach in short cues in the air; teaching at the wrong time or altitude creates hazards [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

To test understanding, vary it: roll out into the wind or across it instead of toward an object [[24:213|AFH 10-4]], or end over a field at the key position [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. Learners who only memorized the pattern usually cannot vary it [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

callout.text: Clear. Heat, idle, glide. Point, roll, steep downwind, shallow upwind. Clear the engine into the wind. Count the loss. Roll out on it.

check.q: Why teach the normal glide, gliding turns and turns around a point before the first steep spiral?
check.a: The spiral is a gliding turn around a point [[24:212|AFH 10-3]], and performance maneuvers should wait until the fundamentals are consistent and be taught in building blocks [[24:210|AFH 10-1]].

body.p: On the CFI test you fly and explain at once. The AIH asks the instructor to explain power settings, attitudes and other factors while demonstrating, and to acknowledge at once any place where the demonstration strays from the explanation [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. In a spiral the words have to keep up with a fast-changing picture.

bullets: The circle comes around quickly. Application of the PHAK rate formula [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]: at 70 knots and 45° of bank, rate = 1,091 x 1 / 70 = 15.6° per second, so one circle through the air takes about 23 seconds. Have short cues ready for each quarter.

Seat and wing: the AFH says the lowered wing of a high-wing airplane can hide the point, especially in left turns from the left seat [[24:154|AFH 7-8]]. Application: from the right seat, expect right turns to hide it from you. Choose altitude and radius so the point stays in view from your seat [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].
Say the altitude at the end of each lap. It shows the examiner your S2 planning and models the AFH habit of noting the loss per revolution [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
Name the moment you clear the engine and the pitch change that goes with it [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
Before the learner takes over, use the three-step exchange of controls you briefed [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

callout.text: Talking takes attention. The AIH warns that an instructor conveying a lot of information can lose track of collision avoidance and situational awareness [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. Application: in a descending spiral, keep the patter short and keep your eyes outside, especially below.

check.q: You are demonstrating a right spiral from the right seat of a high-wing airplane, and the point disappears under your wing on part of each lap. What do you do?
check.a: Change the altitude or the radius so the point stays visible [[24:154|AFH 7-8]], and say so aloud; your learner on the left side may still see it.

chunks.title: Division of attention, distractions and disorientation

body.p: Division of attention between aircraft control and orientation is built into the maneuver. Turns around a point already ask the pilot to divide attention between the flight path, ground references, the controls, outside hazards and the instruments [[24:153|AFH 7-7]]. The spiral adds a fast descent, airspeed control, engine clearing and an altitude count.

bullets: Fixation: absorption in one task while the others slip. It often means the task got too little practice on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Application: eyes glued to the point while the speed and bank wander, or glued to the airspeed indicator while the circle drifts.
How to spot it: follow the learner's eyes; a long stare at one thing suggests fixation [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

Task prioritization: make sure each task can be done reasonably well alone before combining them [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Airborne, budgeting time and prioritizing tasks leave room to work without error [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

Loss of situational awareness: it covers the airplane's position, flight path, other aircraft and the environment [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. Application: which lap, which way the wind blows, how far above the floor.

Distractions that fit this Task: the AIH list includes identifying terrain or objects on the ground and identifying a field suitable for a forced landing [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. Avoid the head-down ones mid-spiral; a head movement in a long turn can bring on the Coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

body.p: Disorientation: in a long, coordinated, constant-rate turn, a pilot can lose the sense of turning. Seeing the altitude drop, the pilot thinks the wings are level, pulls back, and tightens the spiral, losing more altitude: the graveyard spiral [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]] [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. The steep spiral is a long descending turn, so practice it only with a good horizon and outside references. Becoming disoriented is a listed steep spiral error [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

callout.text: Orientation check (application): right after the rollout, ask 'Where is the wind from, and which way is our field?' A learner who cannot answer flew the circle by habit, not by awareness.

check.q: On lap three your learner stares at the point, the bank is wandering and the speed is 14 knots fast. What is happening and what do you coach?
check.a: Fixation [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Coach a scan: point, nose and wings against the horizon, airspeed, traffic, and lead each bank change with pitch [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

body.p: Collision hazards: the steep spiral starts with clearing the airspace for traffic and hazards [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. The AFH's ground reference chapter calls for two 90° clearing turns, looking left and right as well as above and below [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. A clearing turn makes sure the next maneuver does not head into another airplane's path; the instructor should teach a clearing procedure and insist on it [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

bullets: Below matters most here. The AFH has simulated emergency descents flown in a turn so the pilot can check for traffic below, and says a radio call announcing the descent may be appropriate [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. Application: the spiral descends through thousands of feet of other people's airspace in a few minutes.
Have the learner say the clearing aloud: 'clear left, right, above, and below' [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
Scan in eye movements of no more than 10°, about 1 second each [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
Traffic that shows no relative motion and stays in one scan quadrant is likely on a collision course [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Practice areas can be crowded and hazy; tell the learner you both own the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].
Pick the area away from open-air assemblies, congested areas and livestock, and watch for towers and wires [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

body.p: Teach the habit, not just the turns. A learner who thinks the instructor does all the looking never builds it, and any start of a maneuver without a traffic check needs correcting at once. In the AIH midair study, instructors were aboard in 37 percent of the collisions [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

callout.text: Not scanning for other traffic during the maneuver is a listed steep spiral error [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Application: the lowered wing blocks part of the sky on every lap, so the scan has to keep moving.

check.q: Why does a steep spiral call for a harder look below than a steep turn does?
check.a: It descends quickly through the airspace below; the AFH flies simulated emergency descents in a turn for the same reason, to check for traffic below [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

chunks.title: Low altitude, stall, spin, CFIT and uncoordinated flight

body.p: Low altitude maneuvering: the ACS requires enough altitude for at least three 360° turns and a finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS AI.IX.B.S2, S6). No source gives the altitude lost per turn; it depends on the airplane, bank and speed. Measure it on the first lap, as the AFH suggests noting the loss on each revolution [[24:213|AFH 10-4]], and plan the start from it.

bullets: Stall and spin: a gliding steep turn near the ground with rudder into the bank and back pressure to hold altitude can turn into an unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Cross-controlling during gliding turns near the ground is a listed descent error [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].
Stall speed rises with load factor in a steep bank [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]; know the POH stall speed at the steepest bank you expect [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

Controlled flight into terrain (CFIT): an airworthy airplane under the pilot's control flown into terrain, an obstacle or water [[30:73|RMH G-1]]. CFIT is one of the top four causes of general aviation fatal accidents [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. Application: in a spiral it looks like a learner fixed on the point while the altimeter runs past the floor.
Uncoordinated flight: powered-flight rudder habits in a glide cause slips and skids [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].
Lower altitudes mean less time to configure and less glide distance if the engine really quits [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

body.p: Do not teach at the wrong altitude: the AIH example is stalls taught below a cloud layer that leaves too little room to recover [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Application: brief a hard rollout altitude above the 1,500-foot floor, and say it aloud on the last lap.

callout.text: A spiral that is turning into a dive near the floor is not the time to save the maneuver. Roll out and recover; the ACS floor is a limit, not a target (application).

check.q: Your learner's third lap ends at 1,620 feet AGL, but the rollout to the assigned heading finishes at 1,460 feet AGL. Does it meet the standard?
check.a: No. The maneuver must be completed no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS AI.IX.B.S6); the fix is a higher start based on the measured loss per turn [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

body.p: The AFH lists ten common steep spiral errors [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Several gliding turn errors from AFH 3-24 show up inside them [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. For S7 the examiner will fly some of these; name what you see, explain the cause and give the fix.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Not clearing the area
Throttle to idle and roll-in with no clearing turns or look below
Insist on a clearing procedure before every maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]
Inadequate pitch control on entry or rollout
Speed jumps at entry because the nose dropped before the airplane slowed, or decays because it was not lowered; nose pitches up at rollout
Slow to gliding speed first, then lower the nose as you roll in [[24:213|AFH 10-4]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]; release the turn's back pressure on rollout [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Not correcting the bank angle to compensate for wind
Same bank all the way around; circle slides downwind
Steepen downwind, shallow upwind [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]; heading ahead of position in the downwind half [[24:154|AFH 7-8]]
Poor flight control coordination
Ball off center; too much rudder in the glide
Lighter rudder in a glide [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]; slight left rudder may be needed [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Ineffective use of trim
Heavy held back pressure; speed wanders when attention moves
Trim once the speed is stable [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]
Inadequate airspeed control
Fast downwind, slow upwind, every lap
Anticipate a pitch change with each bank change [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]
Becoming disoriented
Loses track of the wind side, the lap count or the rollout heading
Brief wind, laps and rollout reference before entry [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]; call each lap aloud (application)
Performing by reference to the flight instruments rather than visual references
Eyes inside on the airspeed indicator or altimeter
Point, nose and horizon outside, instruments as a cross-check; watch the learner's eyes [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]
Not scanning for other traffic during the maneuver
Head still, eyes on the point
A traffic scan every lap, below included [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]
Not completing the turn on the designated heading or reference
Rollout more than 10° off (ACS AI.IX.B.S6)
Lead the rollout; the lead depends on the type of turn, rate of turn and rollout rate [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]

body.p: How to analyze: decide whether an error comes from a misconception or from motor skill; a learner who talks while flying shows you which [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Safety permitting, let the learner go part of the way into a mistake and find the way out [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]; in the spiral, set that limit by altitude and bank before the flight. If it needs reteaching, demonstrate again, let the learner practice under direction, then evaluate [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

callout.text: Read the circle: if it drifts away from the point on the downwind side, the bank there is too shallow, because a higher groundspeed widens a fixed-bank turn [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

check.q: As your learner, the examiner holds 45° all the way around and the circle creeps downwind each lap. Which listed error is it, and what is your fix?
check.a: Not correcting the bank angle to compensate for wind [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Steepen on downwind headings and shallow on upwind headings to hold the radius [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

f1.alt: A high-wing airplane enters at upper left and flies three descending, stacked orange circles around a runway below, banking steeply in each circle, then rolls out along an arrow to the right. The shadow of one constant-radius circle lies on the ground around the runway. A blue arrow at the bottom marks the wind.

f2.alt: A top-down view of an orange circle around a clump of trees, with the wind blowing from the top. Labels show the steepest bank where the airplane heads downwind, the shallowest bank where it heads upwind, a steeper bank and a shallower bank in between, and dashed lines marking the upwind and downwind halves of the circle.

f3.alt: Four panels, A to D, each a top-down view of an airplane flying left to right along a straight road and making a 360° turn. A: no wind, the loop closes back over the road. B: wind blowing along the road toward the left, against the airplane's direction, so the turn starts into the wind and the loop ends back over the road farther left (downwind). C: wind blowing across the road, the loop carries the airplane off to the downwind side. D: wind blowing along the road in the airplane's direction. Small insets show the airplane's attitude.

f6.alt: A five-row table titled Spiral Dive Recovery Template: 1, reduce power (throttle) to idle; 2, apply some forward elevator; 3, roll wings level; 4, gently raise the nose to level flight; 5, increase power to climb power.

f7.alt: Two paths from an airplane at the top: a brown curve labeled graveyard spiral that sweeps down and around, and blue tight coils labeled graveyard spin that end in a crash burst. A second airplane at lower left heads away along a brown arrow.

scenario.title: Re-teaching the spiral after a failed stage check
scenario.setup: You are a CFI. Your commercial learner just failed the steep spiral on a school stage check: the circle drifted, the airspeed ran 15 knots fast on every downwind side, and the rollout ended at 1,400 feet AGL. Today you fly a carbureted high-wing trainer. The air is 55°F and humid, the wind at altitude is about 20 knots from the north, and the practice area is farmland at 900 feet MSL with a lone silo, a few miles from a VOR.

questions.q: Before you fly again, what goes into the ground briefing?
questions.a: The objective and standard and the safety procedures [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]; the cause behind each stage check error (bank not changed for wind, pitch not led with bank, no altitude plan) [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]; who controls the throttle [[24:200|AFH 9-29]]; and the exchange of controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

questions.q: How do you pick the starting altitude today?
questions.a: Fly one lap yourself and note the loss [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. If it is about 600 feet, three turns need 1,800 feet above the 1,500-foot AGL floor over 900-foot ground: 900 + 1,500 + 1,800 = 4,200 feet MSL, plus a margin (ACS AI.IX.B.S2, S6).

questions.q: What is your engine plan for the long idle glide in this weather?
questions.a: 55°F and humid is inside the carburetor icing chart [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. Full carburetor heat before closing the throttle, left on, and clear the engine for a few seconds periodically [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]], headed north into the wind with pitch adjusted for constant airspeed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

questions.q: Headed south, the circle bulges away from the silo and the learner's bank is still 40°. What do you say?
questions.a: South is downwind with a north wind, so groundspeed is highest and the bank must be steepest there [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]; a fixed bank at higher groundspeed widens the circle [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]. Keep the steepest bank at or below 60° (ACS AI.IX.B.S4).

questions.q: The learner steepens and the speed builds again, as on the stage check. How do you fix it for good?
questions.a: Show that each bank increase needs a pitch increase, because gliding turns need more back pressure [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] and airspeed changes with bank [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Teach the sound cue too [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. If the error persists, demonstrate again, then supervise practice [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

questions.q: On lap two you spot a trainer below, climbing toward your altitude near the VOR. What now?
questions.a: Traffic clusters near VORs [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]], and a target with no relative motion is likely on a collision course [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]. Stop the spiral, roll out and keep the traffic in sight; both of you own the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

skills.do: Clear the area, especially below, before the demonstration and explain the clearing as you do it.
skills.practice: Fly two 90° clearing turns looking left, right, above and below before every spiral, and call it aloud [[24:148|AFH 7-2]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

skills.do: Select an altitude sufficient to continue through a series of at least three, 360° turns, and explain how you chose it from the loss per turn and the 1,500-foot AGL floor.
skills.practice: Measure the altitude lost per lap in your training airplane at your usual bank and speed, and keep the number in your kneeboard [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

skills.do: Establish and maintain a steep spiral, never past 60° of bank, at a constant radius about a suitable ground reference point, while explaining power, pitch and bank.
skills.practice: Practice the roll-in at the point and the patter for each quarter until talking costs no airspeed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]] [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

skills.do: Apply wind-drift correction to hold a constant radius circle, with the bank not past 60° at its steepest point, and explain why the bank changes.
skills.practice: Fly the AFH road demonstration in wind, then spirals sized so the downwind bank stays well under 60° [[24:150|AFH 7-4]] [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

skills.do: Divide attention between airplane control, traffic avoidance and the ground track while staying coordinated, and say what you are looking at.
skills.practice: Have another pilot call out traffic and ball position while you narrate; work on lighter rudder in the glide [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

skills.do: Maintain the specified airspeed ±10 knots, roll out toward an object or specified heading ±10°, and complete the maneuver no lower than 1,500 feet AGL.
skills.practice: Practice rollouts directly into the wind and perpendicular to it, and lead each bank change with pitch [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task: watch the examiner fly a flawed spiral, name the error, explain its cause, give the fix, and take control if safety requires.
skills.practice: Have a fellow applicant fly each AFH error on purpose while you diagnose it aloud [[24:213|AFH 10-4]] [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, what does the distance from the reference point at the roll-in establish?
options: The turning radius of the spiral
The steepest bank angle allowed
The gliding speed for the descent
The altitude lost on each lap
quiz.why: The pilot should consider the distance from the reference point, since it establishes the turning radius [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

quiz.q: In the AFH road demonstration, you fly into the wind along a road and make a 360° turn at a constant medium bank. Where do you end up?
options: Off the road, on the crosswind side
Over the road, exactly at the point where it started
Over the road, upwind of the start
Over the road, downwind of the start
quiz.why: With the road parallel to the wind, the airplane returns directly over the road but downwind of the starting point [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

quiz.q: Which three things does the AFH say tend to force the nose down and raise the speed in a gliding turn?
options: Tilted lift, excess rudder, power-off nose-down stability
Tilted lift, P-factor, carburetor heat use
Trim drift, flap drag, propeller windmilling
Headwind, groundspeed loss, density altitude
quiz.why: The three are the decrease in lift from the tilted lift force, excessive rudder from reduced control pressures, and the airplane's normal nose-down tendency with power off [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

quiz.q: Why do learners often skid in the gliding turns of a steep spiral?
options: Carburetor heat adds a strong left yaw
P-factor is strongest when the throttle is closed
They use the rudder pressure they learned with power on
The rudder loses most of its authority at gliding speed, so they push harder
quiz.why: Rudder pressures are reduced in a glide, and learners may apply excessive pressure based on powered flight, causing slips and skids [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

quiz.q: When does the PHAK say to apply carburetor heat if icing is suspected and you plan a long idle descent?
options: Full on before closing the throttle, and left on
Half on after the throttle is closed, then full on at the rollout
Full on only if the rpm starts to drop
Full on at rollout, before power is added
quiz.why: Adjust carburetor heat to full on before closing the throttle and leave it on during closed-throttle operation [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

quiz.q: In a simulated emergency, what does the AFH say about control of the throttle?
options: The instructor always keeps one hand on it
The pilot controls it, but the instructor clears the engine
Either the instructor or the pilot has complete control, with no doubt
Both pilots share it and call each change
quiz.why: Either the instructor or the pilot should have complete control of the throttle; many near accidents came from misunderstandings [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

quiz.q: Which of these is a common error in spiral dive recovery listed by the AFH?
options: Rolling the wings fully level before raising the nose to level flight
Pulling out of the dive while rolling wings level
Reducing power to idle as the first step
Applying climb power once the speed is VY
quiz.why: Simultaneously pulling out of the dive while rolling wings level is a listed error; the other three are parts of the correct procedure [[24:131|AFH 5-26]] [[24:132|AFH 5-27]].

quiz.q: Which distraction from the AIH list fits a steep spiral lesson best?
options: Get something from the back seat and hand it forward
Identify a field suitable for a forced landing
Drop a pencil and pick it up
Compute true airspeed on a flight computer
quiz.why: Identifying a field for a forced landing is on the AIH list [[25:180|AIH 9-10]] and ties to the spiral's purpose [[24:212|AFH 10-3]]. Head-down tasks in a long turn invite the Coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH say about the base key position when teaching power-off approaches?
options: Fly it at 1,000 feet AGL over a fixed point
Always use the same tree or crossroad so the learner can find it
Vary it in altitude and location; it is not a landmark
Use it only for the 90° power-off approach
quiz.why: The base key position should not be thought of as a particular landmark; altitude and location should be varied as much as practical [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

quiz.q: Which of these is on the AFH list of common steep spiral errors?
options: Not lowering the first notch of flaps at the start of the first lap
Rolling out with the carburetor heat still on
Using more than 45° of bank at any point
Not correcting the bank angle to compensate for wind
quiz.why: Not correcting the bank angle to compensate for wind is error 3 of 10 [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

final_quiz.q: During S7 the examiner, as your learner, finishes at 1,540 feet AGL, rolls out 6° off the assigned heading, peaks at 57° of bank and runs 11 knots fast. What do you call out as outside the standard?
options: The final altitude
The rollout heading
The steepest bank
The airspeed
final_quiz.why: The standard is the specified airspeed ±10 knots, rollout ±10°, no lower than 1,500 feet AGL, and no more than 60° of bank (ACS AI.IX.B.S3, S4, S6). Only the 11 knots is outside. Airspeed control is a listed error [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner says: 'I was at 60° headed downwind and still drifting outside the circle.' What do you teach for the next try?
options: Hold 65° briefly on the downwind side, then shallow out again
Roll in farther from the point, so the circle is bigger and the downwind bank shallower
Hold one constant bank so the downwind drift is easier to see
Add rudder toward the point to skid the nose back inside the circle
final_quiz.why: The distance from the point sets the radius, and the steepest bank must not exceed 60° [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. A bigger radius needs less bank at the same groundspeed [[24:150|AFH 7-4]]. Skidding a gliding turn invites a spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner rolls out of the spiral and the nose rises; the speed decays toward the stall warning. What is the most likely cause?
options: The learner added too much right rudder
The carburetor heat was turned off too early during the rollout
The wind shifted to a headwind on rollout
The back pressure used in the turn was not released
final_quiz.why: Recovering from a gliding turn, the back pressure applied in the turn must be decreased or the airplane may pitch up and lose airspeed [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

final_quiz.q: You fly the AFH road demo with a crosswind and the airplane ends up well off the road. Your learner says you must have changed the bank. What do you explain?
options: The bank never changed; the air moved, so the track was not a circle
The road was not straight, so nothing can be learned from it
You did steepen it a little, which is why the turn ended off the road
Crosswind changes airspeed, and that made the circle drift
final_quiz.why: With a crosswind, the same constant-bank turn drifts away from the road; the path over the ground is not circular even though the turn through the air was perfect [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

final_quiz.q: Using the AFH example: a 45° bank at 100 knots groundspeed gives an 890-foot circle downwind. If the learner keeps 45° all the way around, what happens at the upwind point, where groundspeed is about 80 knots?
options: Nothing changes, because the bank angle stayed the same
The circle tightens, so the airplane cuts inside the radius
The circle widens, so the airplane drifts outside the radius
The airspeed rises 20 knots to hold the same radius
final_quiz.why: As groundspeed decreases, the radius at a fixed bank decreases [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]; the AFH says to shallow to about 33° at the upwind point [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner clears the engine on the downwind side at the steepest bank, without touching pitch, and the speed jumps. What do you coach?
options: Clear it downwind, but reduce the bank while doing so
Clear it only after the rollout to keep the circle clean
Clear it headed into the wind, adjusting pitch to hold airspeed
Stop clearing the engine; it is optional on a spiral of only three turns
final_quiz.why: Advance the throttle periodically for a few seconds, adjusting pitch for a constant airspeed, preferably when headed into the wind [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

final_quiz.q: On the first spiral your learner rolls in and the speed decays 8 knots below gliding speed. Which listed gliding turn error is this?
options: Not lowering the pitch at gliding turn entry
Not slowing to glide speed before lowering the nose
Using too much rudder during the recovery
Not stabilizing the glide before trimming
final_quiz.why: Failure to lower pitch attitude during gliding turn entry, resulting in a decrease in airspeed, is a listed error [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]; the spiral lowers the pitch as the bank goes in [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

final_quiz.q: Lap four, hazy horizon. Your learner says 'we're level now' and starts pulling back while the altimeter keeps unwinding. What is the best response?
options: Let the learner keep pulling, since back pressure is what stops a descent like this
Have the learner tighten the turn to get around to the heading
Add full power first so the airplane climbs out of the turn
Unload, roll wings level, then gently raise the nose; take over if needed
final_quiz.why: Pulling back in a graveyard spiral tightens it and increases the altitude loss [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. Spiral dive recovery: idle, some forward elevator, roll level, gently raise the nose [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Take control calmly when necessary [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner flies a tidy spiral around the same silo every lesson. How do you find out if they understand it?
options: Have them fly the same spiral around the same silo five more times in a row to be sure
Ask them to recite the ACS tolerances from memory
Fly a demo yourself and ask them to grade it
Ask for a rollout directly into the wind or a spiral to the key position over a field
final_quiz.why: Learners who do not understand the principles usually cannot vary the maneuver or combine it with others [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Rolling out into the wind [[24:213|AFH 10-4]] or spiraling to the key position [[24:199|AFH 9-28]] are good variations.

final_quiz.q: During your learner's spiral you reach over and advance the throttle to clear the engine without saying anything. What risk does the AFH warn about?
options: Advancing the throttle at idle can shock-cool the engine
Only the pilot in the left seat may move the throttle
Confusion over who controls the throttle has caused many near accidents
Clearing the engine is not allowed during a spiral
final_quiz.why: There should be no doubt who controls the throttle in a simulated emergency, since many near accidents have come from such misunderstandings [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].

final_quiz.q: The field below is at 1,100 feet MSL. Your demo lost about 700 feet per turn. What is the lowest MSL altitude to start three turns and still meet the ACS floor?
options: 3,600 feet MSL
4,700 feet MSL
4,000 feet MSL
5,400 feet MSL
final_quiz.why: Three turns at 700 feet = 2,100 feet. 1,100 + 1,500 + 2,100 = 4,700 feet MSL, before any margin (ACS AI.IX.B.S2, S6). The AFH suggests noting the loss per revolution [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

final_quiz.q: Air at 50°F and humid. Late in the spiral, the learner clears the engine and it runs rough with low rpm. What do you have the learner do?
options: Partial carburetor heat, so the engine does not lose any more of its power
Carburetor heat off so the engine gets dense air
Full carburetor heat, left full on until normal power returns
Lean the mixture and keep the throttle at idle
final_quiz.why: Carburetor ice can build unnoticed in a reduced-power descent; apply full heat and keep it full hot until normal power returns, resisting the urge to reduce it [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your commercial learner wants to practice steep spirals with a non-pilot friend aboard and no parachutes. What does 14 CFR 91.307 allow?
options: It is legal if no intentional maneuver exceeds 60° of bank or 30° of pitch
It is legal only above 1,500 feet AGL, the ACS floor for the maneuver
Nothing; any steep spiral with a passenger aboard needs parachutes for everyone
It is legal at any bank, since the steep spiral is a required commercial maneuver
final_quiz.why: The parachute rule applies only to intentional maneuvers exceeding 60° of bank or 30° nose-up or nose-down; the required-maneuver exception covers instruction given by a CFI or ATP, not practice with a friend [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]]. The spiral standard caps bank at 60° (ACS AI.IX.B.S3).

takeaways: Purpose: lose lots of altitude fast while staying over one spot, the way an engine-out pilot reaches the key position over a field.
Standard: bank never past 60°, specified airspeed ±10 knots, rollout ±10°, at least three turns, finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL.
Bank follows groundspeed: steepest headed downwind, shallowest headed upwind. Size the circle for the wind.
Every bank change is a pitch change; gliding turns need more back pressure and lighter rudder.
Carb heat before idle, clear the engine headed into the wind, and settle who has the throttle.
Clear below, count the loss per lap, and roll out early rather than break the floor.
If it turns into a dive: idle, unload, roll level, then raise the nose gently.
cfi_notes: ACS S4 reads 'with bank not to exceed 60° a steepest point in turn' (ACS AI.IX.B.S4); the commercial ACS has the same wording (ACS CA.V.B.S4). Read it as 'at the steepest point' and quote it as written if asked.

AFH 7-2 gives 45° as a general bank limit for ground reference maneuvers [[24:148|AFH 7-2]], while the steep spiral allows up to 60° at the steepest point [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Learners coming from turns around a point need to hear which number applies here.

AFH 7-4 says the bank for a constant ground radius is 'proportional to groundspeed' [[24:150|AFH 7-4]]. It is not strictly linear; the PHAK radius formula [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]] with groundspeed in it reproduces the AFH's own 890-foot, 45° and 33° numbers (application).

The AFH has turns around a point entered downwind [[24:154|AFH 7-8]], but the steep spiral text only says to roll in as the reference point is reached [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Application: entering on the downwind side puts the steepest bank first, while the learner is fresh.

The steep spiral text gives no rollout lead. The AIH says the lead depends on the type of turn, turn rate and rollout rate [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]; in a gliding spiral with a changing bank, teach the learner to judge it from the actual bank.

The AIH distraction list includes dropping a pencil and reaching into the back seat [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]; in a long descending turn those head movements invite the Coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Use ground-reference distractions instead, such as naming a forced landing field.

The sources give load factor and stall speed only for level turns [[24:211|AFH 10-2]]; none gives the load factor in a descending spiral. Use the level-turn figures as a guide and compare the POH stall speed at the steepest bank with your gliding speed [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

The private ACS has no steep spiral, so a commercial learner may meet it new. Spiraling down over a field is already part of simulated emergency landings [[24:199|AFH 9-28]], which gives you a known-to-unknown bridge [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

The AFH explains the hidden point only for left turns from the left seat [[24:154|AFH 7-8]]. From the right seat it reverses (application), so plan your demo direction and do not assume the learner sees what you see.
gaps: No source gives the altitude lost per turn or the descent rate in a steep spiral; measure it in your airplane [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
The ACS does not define the 'specified airspeed'; the AFH says gliding speed [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. The POH/AFM gives that speed, and the examiner may specify another.
The AFH steep spiral text does not address flaps; Figure 9-28 shows flaps retracted for the spiral down to a field [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. Follow the POH/AFM.
How often and how long to clear the engine is not quantified beyond 'periodically' and 'a few seconds' [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]; check the POH/AFM for engine guidance.
No source says how far an instructor should let a spiral error develop before taking control; the AIH only says 'safety permitting' [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

activities.title: Recover the spiral that became a dive
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the recovery steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Apply some forward elevator to unload to about +1 G
Roll wings level with coordinated aileron and rudder
Gently raise the nose to level flight
At VY, apply climb power and climb back to a safe altitude

activities.title: Size the circle for the wind
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer. Radius = groundspeed squared / (11.26 x tangent of bank).

items.q: AFH example: 90 knots airspeed in a 10-knot wind, an 888-foot circle (45° at 100 knots groundspeed downwind, about 33° upwind). Halfway around, the wind is straight across and the groundspeed is about the airspeed, 90 knots. What bank holds the circle there?
items.why: tan bank = 90 x 90 / (11.26 x 888) = 8,100 / 9,999 = 0.810. Bank = 39.0°, between the downwind 45° and the upwind 33° [[24:150|AFH 7-4]] [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]. With the wind across the nose, its effect on groundspeed is small [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

items.q: Your gliding speed is 70 knots TAS and the wind at altitude is 15 knots. What is the groundspeed headed directly downwind?
items.why: 70 + 15 = 85 knots. Headed downwind the groundspeed is higher than the airspeed [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

items.q: You want no more than 50° of bank at that 85-knot downwind point. What radius over the ground does that give?
Same 538-foot circle. Headed upwind the groundspeed is 70 - 15 = 55 knots. What bank holds the radius there?
Lower down the wind picks up to 25 knots, so the downwind groundspeed is 95 knots. What bank now holds the same 538-foot circle downwind?
items.why: tan bank = 95 x 95 / (11.26 x 538) = 9,025 / 6,058 = 1.490. Bank = 56.1°, close to the 60° limit (ACS AI.IX.B.S4). Keep correcting for wind changes [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

activities.title: True or false: traffic and the area
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The AFH ground reference chapter calls for two 90° clearing turns, looking left, right, above and below.
In the AIH midair study, most collisions happened in poor visibility.
cards.why: False. Most occurred in VFR weather, in daylight, with visibility greater than 3 miles [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

cards.s: A radio call announcing your descent intentions may be appropriate before a descent in a busy area.
cards.why: True. The AFH says so for emergency descents, which are also flown in a turn to check for traffic below [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

cards.s: Traffic that keeps the same spot in your windshield and grows larger is no threat because it is not moving.
cards.why: False. No relative motion while staying in one scan quadrant means a likely collision course; if it grows larger, take evasive action [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

cards.s: Ground reference practice areas should be well away from open-air assemblies, congested areas and livestock.
Once the learner can fly the spiral, the instructor can take over all the scanning.
cards.why: False. Learners who think the instructor does all the scanning never build the habit [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]; you both own the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

activities.title: Teaching the first steep spiral
activities.intro: You are the CFI. Your commercial learner is flying a carbureted high-wing trainer. The air is 55°F and humid, the wind at altitude is about 20 knots from the north, and the practice area is farmland at 900 feet MSL with a lone silo for a reference.

steps.s: On the ground the learner plans to start at 3,000 feet MSL 'because that is where we do steep turns.'
options: Accept it, since steep turns and spirals both use the same altitude block
Plan from the loss per turn: three turns and the 1,500-foot AGL floor above the 900-foot ground, with margin
Start at 2,400 feet MSL so the learner gets used to lower altitudes
Ignore the altitude now and fix it in the air if needed
steps.why: The ACS requires altitude for at least three 360° turns and a finish no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS AI.IX.B.S2, S6). 3,000 MSL is only 2,100 AGL here. Note the loss per revolution to plan [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].

steps.s: Over the silo the learner closes the throttle first and then reaches for the carburetor heat.
options: Let it go, since the order does not matter at idle
Use partial carburetor heat to limit the power loss
Tell the learner to skip carburetor heat to keep more power
Coach heat first, then throttle, and leave the heat on during the glide
steps.why: With icing conditions suspected and closed-throttle operation planned, apply full heat before closing the throttle and leave it on [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

steps.s: The learner rolls to 40° and holds it. Headed south, the circle bulges away from the silo.
options: Hold 40°; the drift will even out on the next lap
Shallow the bank headed south to let the circle settle
Steepen the bank headed south, where groundspeed is highest
Add right rudder to yaw the nose toward the silo
steps.why: With a north wind, south is downwind: steepen on downwind headings and shallow on upwind headings [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]. Higher groundspeed widens a fixed-bank circle [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

steps.s: Now at 55° headed south, the airspeed is 12 knots above the specified speed.
options: Raise the nose a little to lead the bank change with pitch
Add a little power to smooth the descent
Accept it; the ACS allows ±15 knots
Reduce the bank to 30° at once
steps.why: Airspeed fluctuates with bank, so anticipate pitch corrections [[24:213|AFH 10-4]]; gliding turns need more back pressure [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. The standard is ±10 knots (ACS AI.IX.B.S6).

steps.s: End of lap three at 1,800 feet AGL, but the rollout heading is still three-quarters of a turn away and each lap has cost about 600 feet.
options: Roll out now and recover, then debrief the altitude plan
Continue to the assigned heading even if below 1,500 feet AGL
Steepen past 60° to get around faster
Keep circling at idle until the heading comes up
steps.why: Three-quarters of a turn at about 600 feet is roughly 450 feet, which ends near 1,350 feet AGL, below the floor (ACS AI.IX.B.S6). Bank may not pass 60° (ACS AI.IX.B.S3, S4). The AFH ties the loss per revolution to the rollout decision [[24:213|AFH 10-4]].
